privacy.title: Privacy Policy
privacy.subtitle: What Improv Toolbox collects, and what it doesn't.

short.title: The short version
items: No account or login. You identify yourself only if you choose to send a message.
Your settings and saved items stay on your device.
Usage analytics are anonymous and not used for ads or tracking.
Optional tips go through Apple or Google. We never see your card.
No data selling, no ads, no cross-app tracking.

noServer.title: No accounts
noServer.body: Improv Toolbox runs on your device. There is no sign-up, no profile, and no server keeping a record of what you do in the tools. Every tool works offline. Only the optional contact form sends the message you write to an external service.

local.title: What stays on your device
local.body: Your language choice, light or dark theme, favorite tools, and anything a tool generates live in your browser's local storage on the web, or in the app's local storage on mobile. This data never leaves your device, and clearing your browser or deleting the app erases it.

analytics.title: Anonymous usage analytics
analytics.web: On the website we use Vercel Analytics and Speed Insights to count visits and measure page speed. They set no cookies and store no personal data. We see aggregate numbers, never individual people.
analytics.app: In the mobile app we use Aptabase, a privacy-first analytics tool. It sends anonymous usage events such as app opens, with no device ID, no advertising ID, no cookies, no fingerprinting, and no long-term user identification. It tells us roughly how the app is used.

purchases.title: Purchases and tips
purchases.body: The mobile app includes an optional tip jar. Apple's App Store or Google Play take the payment, and RevenueCat validates and records the purchase. RevenueCat receives purchase history, store transaction details, product and price information, an anonymous app user ID for your install, and coarse store/device details such as country, locale, currency, and platform. We do not send RevenueCat your name, email, or any custom customer attributes. RevenueCat never receives your card number from us, and we never see your card. The website links to Buy Me a Coffee instead, which keeps its own privacy policy.

messages.title: Messages you send us
messages.body: The contact form is optional. On the website and in the iOS and Android apps, the name you provide, your email address, the selected topic, and your message are sent to Formspree so it can deliver the message to us and protect the form from spam. Formspree also receives technical request data such as your IP address and browser or app information. Free-plan submissions remain available in our Formspree dashboard for 30 days. We use this information only to read and reply to your message.

providers.title: Service providers
items: Vercel: website hosting, anonymous traffic analytics, and page-speed measurement.
Aptabase: anonymous usage analytics in the mobile app.
RevenueCat: purchase history and receipt validation for in-app tips on mobile.
Formspree: delivery, spam protection, and temporary storage of messages sent through the contact form.
Apple App Store and Google Play: app payment processing under their own policies.

store.title: Mobile app store disclosures
store.body: For App Store and Google Play privacy forms, the mobile app declares Usage Data / Product Interaction for Aptabase analytics and Purchases / Purchase History for RevenueCat in-app tips. If you choose to use the contact form, it also declares your name, email address, and message as data linked to you and used only for app functionality and support. We do not use this data for advertising, cross-app tracking, or data brokerage.

never.title: What we never do
never.body: We don't sell or rent your data. We don't run ads. We don't track you across other apps or websites, and we don't build a profile of you.

rights.title: Your rights
rights.body: Most app data stays on your device. To remove local data, clear your browser storage or uninstall the app. Anonymous Aptabase analytics cannot be tied back to you, so there is no individual analytics profile to export or delete. For contact messages or RevenueCat tip-purchase data, email us with enough detail to identify the record, and we will handle access or deletion where possible. Formspree, Apple, and Google may retain records under their own policies. If you have a request under the GDPR or a similar law, email us.

children.title: Children
children.body: Improv Toolbox is built for a general audience and does not require accounts. The optional contact form is not intended for children to submit personal information, and we do not knowingly collect personal data from children. Some store age ratings may reflect mild text prompts such as horror genre or dramatic themes.

changes.title: Changes
changes.body: If this policy changes, we'll update the date at the top of this page. We'll note major changes in the app or on the site.

contact.body: Questions about privacy? Email us at

warmups.title: Warmup Generator
warmups.subtitle: Find the perfect warmup for your group

zip_zap_zop.name: Zip Zap Zop
zip_zap_zop.description: Stand in a tight circle, close enough to point at anyone across from you. One player locks eyes with someone, snaps a hand toward them and says 'Zip'. That person passes it on the same way to anyone else with 'Zap', the next sends 'Zop', and then the word loops back to 'Zip' to start the cycle again. The three words always run in that order; only the direction and the target change. Keep your eye contact sharp and aim the energy straight at whoever you pick. Say the wrong word, break the order, or freeze for too long, and you drop out of the circle (or pay a forfeit like a quick squat) before the next round starts.
zip_zap_zop.tips: Start slow enough for everyone to lock in the Zip-Zap-Zop order, then keep pushing the tempo until it breaks. Once the group is warm, give each word its own exaggerated gesture so the whole body wakes up along with the voice.

yes_and.name: Yes, and...
yes_and.description: Two people build a scene together, but every line MUST start with 'Yes, and...'. The goal: accept what your partner offers and build on that reality without blocking.
yes_and.tips: Make sure the 'yes' is genuine – not 'yes, but'.

sound_ball.name: Sound Ball
sound_ball.description: Imagine a ball. Throw it across the circle with a distinctive sound and gesture. The catcher must mimic your sound when catching, then create a brand new sound and gesture when throwing.
sound_ball.tips: Exaggerate your gestures – it warms up the body and voice at the same time.

freeze_tag.name: Freeze!
freeze_tag.description: Two people play a scene. At any moment, someone from the audience shouts 'Freeze!'. Both actors freeze. The caller enters, taps one actor, takes over their body and position, then starts a completely new scene.
freeze_tag.tips: Enter fast – don't wait for the 'perfect' moment. An interesting body position is your starting point.

mirror.name: Mirror
mirror.description: Pair up and stand an arm's length apart, facing each other like two halves of a reflection. One of you leads with slow, smooth movements: raise a hand, tilt your head, shift your weight. Your partner copies everything at the same instant, as if they were your image in a mirror. Move slowly enough that your partner can stay exactly with you, with no sudden jerks to catch them out. After a minute or so, swap who leads. For the final round, drop the leader role entirely and let the movement pass back and forth on its own, so neither of you decides who starts it.
mirror.tips: Hold each other's gaze instead of staring at the hands, and let your peripheral vision do the tracking. You are succeeding when anyone watching genuinely cannot tell who is leading and who is following.

one_word_story.name: One Word Story
one_word_story.description: Participants take turns adding one word each, building a coherent story together. Forbidden: blocking with 'End.' or deliberately incoherent words. All connectives allowed.
one_word_story.tips: Don't plan ahead – react to your predecessor's word. Accept every direction.

status_walk.name: Status Walk
status_walk.description: Everyone gets a card with a number 1–10 (their status). Without showing the card, walk around the space and form a community according to your statuses. Then find your place in the hierarchy.
status_walk.tips: Details matter: posture, pace, eye contact, tone of voice – these build status.

kitty_wants_a_corner.name: Kitty Wants a Corner
kitty_wants_a_corner.description: One person stands in the middle as the 'kitty'. Everyone else has a spot. The kitty asks someone 'Kitty, can I have your corner?'. If refused, the kitty moves on. Meanwhile, others can swap spots – if the kitty takes a free spot, the displaced person becomes the new kitty.
kitty_wants_a_corner.tips: Speed of swapping is key – make eye contact with others to coordinate your moves.

emotional_replay.name: Emotional Replay
emotional_replay.description: Play a simple, everyday scene (e.g., grocery shopping). Then the facilitator calls out an emotion and the entire scene is replayed in that emotion. Change emotions several times.
emotional_replay.tips: The more mundane the scene topic, the more striking the contrast with the emotion. Don't be afraid of exaggeration.

conducted_story.name: Conducted Story
conducted_story.description: A line of actors tells a story – one at a time. The conductor points at who speaks. When switched, the new person continues exactly where the previous left off – even mid-word.
conducted_story.tips: Speak slowly and clearly. Leave words/sentences open-ended so others can finish them in interesting ways.

name_ball.name: Name Ball
name_ball.description: Stand in a circle. Throw an imaginary ball across the circle, saying the name of the person you're throwing to – before you throw. Start slowly, then speed up. Once everyone knows names, add a second ball.
name_ball.tips: Eye contact BEFORE the throw – don't surprise people. Great for first sessions since it naturally teaches names.

superhero_poses.name: Superhero Poses
superhero_poses.description: Everyone walks around the space. On the facilitator's signal, everyone freezes in a superhero pose and shouts their superpower. Then explore variations: sad superhero, exhausted superhero, confused superhero.
superhero_poses.tips: Encourage exaggerated poses and strong voices. Great for warming up the body and breaking inhibitions at the start of a workshop.

presents.name: Presents
presents.description: In pairs: one person hands their partner an imaginary gift, saying 'I have something for you!' and starting to unwrap it. The partner must identify the object BASED ON SHAPE AND WEIGHT before receiving it. Then swap.
presents.tips: Giver: be precise with your gesture – don't say what it is. Receiver: say what you see before the giver finishes – practice reading physical offers.

space_object.name: Space Object
space_object.description: One person enters and starts working with an imaginary object (e.g., a saw). When another person enters, they must take over that same object and continue – then transform it into something else by changing the action.
space_object.tips: Be specific – size, weight, texture. The transformation must be gradual and fluid, not sudden.

what_are_you_doing.name: What Are You Doing?
what_are_you_doing.description: Person A starts doing an action (e.g., washing dishes). Person B asks: 'What are you doing?' A answers with a DIFFERENT action (e.g., 'Climbing Everest'). B must now perform that action. The next person asks B – and so on.
what_are_you_doing.tips: The response must be instant and absurd. It's forbidden to name the action you're actually performing.

gibberish.name: Gibberish
gibberish.description: Pairs or groups play scenes in a made-up language – no real words allowed. Communication only through tone, rhythm, gestures and facial expression. Variant: one person speaks normally, the other translates in gibberish.
gibberish.tips: Focus on emotion and intention, not on the sound. Gibberish reveals how much meaning is carried by the body and voice versus words alone.

worlds_worst.name: World's Worst
worlds_worst.description: The facilitator names a category (e.g., 'dentist', 'pilot', 'therapist'). Participants take turns entering and showing a one-minute scene as the 'world's worst [profession]'. Goal: be as specific as possible, not just generally bad.
worlds_worst.tips: The best version isn't chaos but a coherent, absurd character with their own logic. Ask yourself: why is this person employed here?

abc_scene.name: ABC Scene
abc_scene.description: Two people play a scene where each line must start with the next letter of the alphabet. A starts with a line beginning with 'A', B responds with 'B', A continues with 'C', and so on until Z.
abc_scene.tips: Focus on the scene, not the letter. The letter should be automatic – that's when the scene has a chance to be truly good.

new_choice.name: New Choice!
new_choice.description: Two people play a scene. The facilitator can call 'New choice!' at any moment. The person who just spoke or acted must immediately replace it with something different. The facilitator can call it multiple times in a row, forcing increasingly strange choices.
new_choice.tips: This exercise trains detachment from your first idea. Advanced version: 'New choice' can even apply to the whole relationship or setting.

emotional_orchestra.name: Emotional Orchestra
emotional_orchestra.description: A group of actors stands in a line. The conductor points to individual people or sections – those actors express the emotion assigned by the conductor (voice, body). The conductor can escalate, quiet down, combine sections.
emotional_orchestra.tips: The conductor should build dramatic arc – not just pick randomly. Actors: listen to the whole orchestra, not just yourself.

harold_opening.name: Harold Opening
harold_opening.description: As a group, build a 'web of associations' from a suggestion word from the audience. Each person adds an image, memory, or idea – NOT directly linked to the previous one, but to the original word or any earlier image. Goal: build rich thematic material.
harold_opening.tips: Don't think too long. Trust the first image that comes to mind. This is an exercise in 'group mind' – the key to long-form improv.

mapping.name: Mapping (Johnstone Status)
mapping.description: The whole group walks around the space. The facilitator assigns each person a hidden status (1–10). Task: find your place in the hierarchy ONLY through observation and reaction – without communicating status directly. Finally: arrange yourselves from lowest to highest.
mapping.tips: This is a sophisticated exercise with a rich history. The key question after: how did you know? The debrief discussion is as important as the exercise itself.

clap_circle.name: Clap Circle
clap_circle.description: Stand in a circle. A clap passes around – one person claps, their neighbor immediately follows. The pace builds until it reaches maximum speed. Variant: change direction on command.
clap_circle.tips: The key is eye contact and readiness – always be prepared to receive the clap.

splat.name: Splat!
splat.description: One person stands in the middle with an imaginary gun. They point at someone and shout 'Splat!'. The targeted person ducks, and their two neighbors must quickly aim at each other and shout 'Splat!'. Last one to react is out.
splat.tips: This trains fast reaction and observation. Mistakes are part of the fun – great for energizing a group.

count_to_twenty.name: Count to Twenty
count_to_twenty.description: The whole group counts to 20 – with no set order and no signals. Only one person can say a number at a time. If two people speak simultaneously, start over from 1. Rule: no non-verbal communication.
count_to_twenty.tips: This exercise is about group awareness and trust. Silence and attention matter more than speed.

three_things.name: Three Things
three_things.description: The facilitator points at someone and names a category (e.g., 'Name three car brands'). The person must list three things as fast as possible. The group claps rhythmically for each one – timing is tight.
three_things.tips: The goal is to bypass the inner censor. Wrong or absurd answers are just as valid – what matters is immediacy.

energy_circle.name: Energy Circle
energy_circle.description: Stand in a circle. One person sends energy (movement + sound) through the center of the circle to a specific person. That person receives it and sends a transformed version to someone else.
energy_circle.tips: Make eye contact before sending. This exercise builds awareness of your partner's offers.

trust_walk.name: Trust Walk
trust_walk.description: Pairs: one person closes their eyes, the other guides them through the space using only light touches (or the closeness of their hand). Then swap. Variant: the guide uses voice only.
trust_walk.tips: Trust is built one small step at a time. Guide: take full responsibility for your partner's safety.

walking_speed.name: Walking Speeds
walking_speed.description: Everyone walks around the space. The facilitator calls a speed from 1 (slow as molasses) through 5 (normal) to 10 (sprinting). Participants adjust without colliding.
walking_speed.tips: Notice how changing speed changes your emotional state. Slow builds tension; fast creates energy and chaos.

blob_tag.name: Blob Tag
blob_tag.description: One person is the 'blob'. When they tag someone, that person joins the blob by holding hands. The blob grows and hunts together. Last free person wins.
blob_tag.tips: The blob must work as a unit – stretching and surrounding. Great for energy and laughs at the start of a workshop.

impulse_pass.name: Impulse Pass
impulse_pass.description: Stand in a circle holding hands. One person squeezes their neighbor's hand – the impulse travels around the circle. When it returns, reverse direction. Variant: multiple impulses at once.
impulse_pass.tips: The goal is group synchronization. End by opening eyes and seeing how fast the impulse can travel.

bus_stop.name: Bus Stop
bus_stop.description: One person sits at the 'bus stop' with a distinct character (age, profession, emotion). Another person joins, playing a different character – contact is inevitable. After a moment the facilitator calls 'Bus!' – the first person boards and leaves. A new person sits down.
bus_stop.tips: Change at least one thing about your character after each interaction. Explore how different characters react to each other.

emotion_walk.name: Emotion Walk
emotion_walk.description: Everyone walks around the space. The facilitator calls an emotion – everyone begins expressing it with their whole body: posture, pace, gaze. Change emotions every 30 seconds. Variant: meet someone in that emotion and feel how it changes the interaction.
emotion_walk.tips: Start with the body, not with thinking about the emotion. Physical expression of emotion is faster and more authentic.

machines.name: Human Machines
machines.description: One person starts a repeating movement with a sound. The next person enters and becomes part of the 'machine' – their movements must connect with the previous person's. Effect: a synchronized, living machine.
machines.tips: Look for connections – your movement can be triggered by your neighbor's. This builds awareness of the group as a system.

dubbing.name: Dubbing
dubbing.description: Pairs or groups of four. Two people play a scene physically (no words). Two others sit with their backs turned and provide the dialogue. Body and voice must together create a character. Then swap.
dubbing.tips: The dubbers: listen to the breath and rhythm of the actors' movements. Synchronization matters more than 'sensible' dialogue.

party_quirks.name: Party Quirks
party_quirks.description: One player hosts a party and steps aside while the rest of the group, or the audience, hands each guest a secret quirk: 'you think you're a dog', 'you've fallen in love with everyone in the room', 'you're slowly turning into your mother'. The host comes back and starts welcoming people into the imaginary living room. Guests arrive one at a time, and each one plays their quirk through how they behave while they chat, fetch a drink, or greet the others. The host keeps the small talk going and works out what is 'off' about each guest, naming a guess out loud whenever a hunch lands. Once the host has pinned down every quirk, the party can wind down.
party_quirks.tips: Play the quirk through what you do, letting it leak into small actions before it takes you over completely, so the host has a trail to follow. Start subtle and crank it up as the host circles closer, and the guessing builds real comic tension.

questions_only.name: Questions Only
questions_only.description: Two people play a scene where they can ONLY speak in questions. Any statement, hesitation, or repetition of the partner's question = out, and someone else takes over.
questions_only.tips: Questions can be rhetorical and emotional. This exercise teaches avoiding blocking through statements and active listening.

sit_stand_lie.name: Sit, Stand, Lie
sit_stand_lie.description: Three people play a scene. At all times EXACTLY one must be sitting, one standing, one lying down. When someone changes position, the others must adjust. The scene must stay coherent despite constant position changes.
sit_stand_lie.tips: Don't pause the scene – position changes are a feature, not an obstacle. Great exercise for creative justification of physicality.

last_letter.name: Last Letter
last_letter.description: Scene for pairs or groups where every line must begin with the last letter of the previous line. E.g., A: 'I love cats.' B: 'So what, cats are boring.' A: 'Good luck convincing me.'
last_letter.tips: Added challenge: no repeating words. Keep your focus on the scene – the letter constraint should become subconscious.

two_line_vocabulary.name: Two-Line Vocabulary
two_line_vocabulary.description: Each character in the scene can only say two specific sentences – chosen before the scene. The entire dialogue is built from only those two phrases per person. Context and emotion must do all the work.
two_line_vocabulary.tips: Choose sentences that fit MANY situations. You'll discover how much tone says versus words.

sound_effect_scene.name: Sound Effect Scene
sound_effect_scene.description: Actors play a scene and create all their own sound effects – ambient sounds, action sounds, atmosphere. One actor can serve as a 'sound center' or each creates their own.
sound_effect_scene.tips: Start with the simplest sounds – footsteps, doors, wind. Synchronization with action matters more than realistic sound.

word_association.name: Word Association Chain
word_association.description: Circle: one person says a word, the next says the first association that comes to mind. No pauses, no thinking. Pace: one word per second.
word_association.tips: If someone hesitates more than a second – 'buzz!', restart from the top. This exercise unlocks spontaneity and disables the inner censor.

four_things.name: Four Things
four_things.description: The facilitator names a category. The pointed-at person must name four specific things from that category – as fast as possible. The group counts out claps: one, two, three, four.
four_things.tips: Categories can get increasingly absurd ('Four things a superhero says on a bus'). Laughter is very much encouraged.

gibberish_translation.name: Gibberish Translator
gibberish_translation.description: Pairs: one person gives a passionate speech in a made-up language (emotionally and with gestures). The other stands beside them and translates line by line into English. The translator must interpret what they see and hear, not invent independently.
gibberish_translation.tips: The translator should follow the emotion and rhythm, not the sounds. The more dramatic the speech, the better the scene.

typewriter.name: Typewriter
typewriter.description: One or two people sit as 'authors'. The rest are 'actors'. The author dictates narration and dialogue. Actors immediately perform it. The author can pause, rewind, or change things.
typewriter.tips: The author should react to what the actors do and build on it, not ignore it. This exercise teaches collaborative narrative creation.

columns.name: Columns
columns.description: Three people stand in a line. Each represents a different theme or voice (e.g., science / love / politics). The facilitator points to which column speaks. Each must continue their own narrative. Effect: three parallel worlds in one scene.
columns.tips: Columns can interact or remain entirely separate. An advanced exercise – requires holding coherence amid constant switching.

space_jump.name: Space Jump
space_jump.description: One person plays a monologue or solo scene. A second person enters with a shout, freezing the action. Both now play a new scene together. A third person enters – and again everything stops for a new context. At the end, unwind the layers back.
space_jump.tips: Each new layer must remember where it was. Returning to previous scenes is the real skill – practice patience and memory.

pattern_game.name: Pattern Game
pattern_game.description: Group stands in a circle. Give a suggestion word. Each person adds an association with the original word (not the previous one). After everyone has gone – return to each person's exact word in the same order. Build a 'pattern' and repeat it at increasing speed.
pattern_game.tips: The goal is to memorize the pattern and reproduce it faster. The foundation of Harold and UCB long-form.

organic_groove.name: Organic Groove
organic_groove.description: The whole group stands in a circle. One person starts a repeating movement with sound. The next adds their own rhythmically compatible one. Gradually the whole group forms a living, synchronized 'groove'. The facilitator can introduce changes.
organic_groove.tips: Listen to the group before joining. Your movement should enrich the whole, not dominate. This exercise builds 'group mind'.

armando.name: Armando
armando.description: One person (Armando) tells a real story from their life. After a moment, actors begin playing scenes inspired by elements of that story – not illustrating it literally, but thematically. Armando periodically returns with another fragment.
armando.tips: Scenes don't need to mirror the story – look for thematic connection. The format teaches working with material 'gifted' by another person.

pan_left_pan_right.name: Pan Left / Pan Right
pan_left_pan_right.description: Three or more people play scenes simultaneously on stage. The facilitator calls 'Pan left!' or 'Pan right!' – the focus (and energy) shifts to the next group, who continue their scene. Each scene must remember where it left off.
pan_left_pan_right.tips: Groups: stay in your scene even when the 'camera' isn't on you. Resumption should be seamless.

slow_motion_replay.name: Slow Motion Replay
slow_motion_replay.description: Play an energetic scene. Then replay it in slow motion – every movement, every word, every emotion. The facilitator can pause and ask for a 'freeze frame' at key moments.
slow_motion_replay.tips: Slowing down reveals impulses that normally remain invisible. This exercise builds body awareness and intentionality.

deconstruction.name: Deconstruction
deconstruction.description: Play a short scene (3–5 minutes). Then 'deconstruct' it: each of three or four groups takes ONE element (character, emotion, image, theme) and builds a new short scene from it. Finally: the whole group combines all the themes.
deconstruction.tips: This format requires analysis and abstraction – use with advanced groups. The debrief afterwards is particularly valuable.

soundscape.name: Soundscape
soundscape.description: The group creates a 'soundscape' for a specific location (forest, harbor, city at night). Each person adds one repeating vocal sound. The facilitator 'conducts' – signaling who to mute or amplify. Variant: an actor enters the soundscape as a character.
soundscape.tips: Start from silence and build slowly. Sounds should be specific and repeatable. The final 'solo' should emerge from the layers.

mind_meld.name: Mind Meld
mind_meld.description: In pairs. Count together 'one, two, three' and on three both players say, out loud and at the same time, the first word that comes to mind. Using those two words as a springboard, count again and both say a new word, trying to land on the same one. Repeat until you both say the identical word.
mind_meld.tips: Pure free association, no strategizing out loud. When you finally match, celebrate it, that shared instinct is exactly the 'group mind' improv runs on.

big_booty.name: Big Booty
big_booty.description: Stand in a circle. One person is 'Big Booty', everyone else numbers off (One, Two, Three...). The group chants a rhythm: 'Big Booty, Big Booty, Big Booty, oh yeah!'. Then Big Booty calls 'Big Booty number Three', Three instantly calls another number, and so on, never breaking the beat. Hesitate or fumble and you go to the end, everyone shifts up.
big_booty.tips: Speed up the chant as you go. The point is failing with a laugh, not winning, keep the energy loose and joyful.

bibbity_bop.name: Bibbity Bibbity Bop
bibbity_bop.description: Stand in a circle with one person in the middle. They point at someone and say either 'Bibbity Bibbity Bop' (the target must say 'Bop' before the caller finishes) or just 'Bop' (the target must stay silent). Mess up and you take the middle. Add group poses, like 'Elephant' or 'Toaster', that the target and their two neighbors must build in three seconds.
bibbity_bop.tips: Keep it fast and add new group poses as you go. It trains instant reaction and joyful failure under pressure.

yes_lets.name: Yes, Let's!
yes_lets.description: Everyone moves freely around the space. At any moment anyone calls out an activity, e.g. 'Let's all paddle a canoe!'. The whole group responds 'Yes, let's!' and immediately does it together. After a few seconds someone proposes the next activity, and the group accepts again.
yes_lets.tips: Accept every offer with full enthusiasm, however silly. This is the purest possible drill for the 'yes, and' reflex and group agreement.

whoosh_bang.name: Whoosh Bang
whoosh_bang.description: Stand in a circle. Pass an energy ball to your neighbor with a 'Whoosh' and a gesture. Anyone can change it: 'Bang' (hands up) bounces it back the other way, 'Groan' sends it across the circle to someone else. Build a small vocabulary of commands and keep the energy flying without dropping the beat.
whoosh_bang.tips: Commit to the sound and the gesture together. Start with two commands and add more only once the group is locked in.

bunny_bunny.name: Bunny Bunny
bunny_bunny.description: Stand in a circle. One person makes 'bunny' hands at their own face singing 'Bunny bunny', then turns to a neighbor singing 'Bunny bunny' to pass it on, while everyone else 'paws' along to the side singing 'Toki toki toki'. The receiver picks it up instantly and passes it on. Keep the rhythm relentless.
bunny_bunny.tips: The whole point is shared rhythm and energy, not getting it 'right'. If it collapses into laughter, you're doing it correctly.

honey_i_love_you.name: Honey, I Love You
honey_i_love_you.description: Sit or stand in a circle. One person is 'it'. They approach anyone, look them in the eye and say 'Honey, I love you, won't you give me a smile?'. The target must reply, deadpan, 'Honey, I love you, but I just can't smile', without smiling or laughing. If they crack, they become 'it'.
honey_i_love_you.tips: No touching, but anything else goes, faces, voices, timing. A great lesson in commitment and holding a straight face under pressure.

alien_tiger_cow.name: Alien, Tiger, Cow
alien_tiger_cow.description: A group version of rock-paper-scissors. On a count of three, everyone strikes one of three poses with its sound: Alien ('bleep bleep', antennae), Tiger ('roar', claws), or Cow ('moo', milking). The goal isn't to beat anyone, it's for the whole group to match the same pose. Keep going until everyone converges.
alien_tiger_cow.tips: Nobody decides out loud, you're reading the room. When the whole group hits the same pose, that's group mind made visible.

space_walk.name: Space Walk
space_walk.description: Everyone walks around the space neutrally. The facilitator calls out an environment or substance, deep snow, hot sand, thick honey, zero gravity, a crowded train, and everyone adjusts how they move through it. Change the world every 30 seconds or so. A Viola Spolin classic for building physical specificity.
space_walk.tips: Commit fully with the whole body, not just your feet. Notice how the imagined environment changes your weight, pace, and even your mood.

i_am_a_tree.name: I Am a Tree
i_am_a_tree.description: One person steps into the space, strikes a pose and says 'I am a tree'. A second adds themselves with a related idea: 'I am a bird in the tree'. A third completes it: 'I am the worm the bird is eating'. Then the first player 'takes' one element with them, and that element restarts the next picture. A group association and tableau builder.
i_am_a_tree.tips: Go with your first instinct rather than the cleverest idea. Each new offer should connect to what's already on stage.

who_started_motion.name: Who Started the Motion
who_started_motion.description: One person, the detective, leaves the room. The circle silently picks a leader who starts a repeating movement (clapping, swaying) that everyone copies. The leader changes the movement every so often and the group follows instantly. The detective returns to the center and has three guesses to spot the leader.
who_started_motion.tips: Followers: don't stare at the leader, use your peripheral vision so you don't give them away. A pure focus and ensemble-awareness drill.

three_headed_expert.name: Three-Headed Expert
three_headed_expert.description: Three players stand shoulder to shoulder as a single 'expert' on any topic the audience names. An interviewer asks questions, and the expert answers one word at a time, each head adding the next word in turn, building sentences nobody planned. The fun is in finishing each other's thoughts coherently.
three_headed_expert.tips: Don't try to steer the sentence, accept whatever word lands before you and add the most natural next one. Punctuate with a clear final word so the interviewer knows you're done.

one_eighty_five.description: A pun game. The group picks a noun, say 'penguins'. Each player in turn delivers the joke: '185 penguins walk into a bar. The bartender says, we don't serve penguins here. The penguins say...' and finishes with a pun on the word. Keep going around until the puns run dry.
one_eighty_five.tips: Groans are as good as laughs, the worse the pun, the better. It trains fast wordplay and committing to a bit that might bomb.

string_of_pearls.name: String of Pearls
string_of_pearls.description: A line of players tells a story out of order. The first player gives the opening sentence, the last player gives the closing sentence. Then players step in one at a time, anywhere in the middle, each adding a single sentence that connects what comes before and after, like threading pearls between two knots, until the story is whole.
string_of_pearls.tips: Every new sentence must honour both ends it sits between. A great bridge from short-form games into long-form narrative thinking.

invocation.name: Invocation
invocation.description: This is a group opening for long-form, run as four passes over a single word the audience gives you. The whole ensemble spreads across the stage and works the word from a new angle each pass. In the first pass you call out literal definitions, each starting 'You are...', as in 'You are a key, you are cold metal, you are the thing I always lose'. In the second you switch to feeling, each line starting 'You make me feel...'. In the third you return to 'You are...' but reach for metaphor and image. In the fourth you speak in the first person and become the thing itself, 'I am...'. Voices overlap and answer each other throughout, and the four passes stack into one shared spoken poem.
invocation.tips: Forget scene and story; your only job is to heighten the images and the feeling around the word. Trust whatever the word pulls up, because the associations you surface here become the raw material the scenes will mine for the rest of the set.

facts.title: Improv Facts
facts.subtitle: Discover the history and techniques of improv

sources.truth_in_comedy: Charna Halpern, Del Close, Kim Johnson – "Truth in Comedy" (1994)
sources.del_close: Del Close, Harold – Annex Theatre, Chicago

history.viola_spolin: Viola Spolin is considered the mother of modern theatrical improv. In 1963 she published "Improvisation for the Theater" – the bible of improv training that still sets the standard for group work today.
history.second_city: The Second City in Chicago, founded in 1959 by students of Viola Spolin, became a star factory: Tina Fey, Stephen Colbert, Steve Carell, Bill Murray, Gilda Radner – they all started there.
history.keith_johnstone: Keith Johnstone developed the status system, masks, and narrative theatre. His book "Impro" (1979) is one of the most important publications on improvisation. Johnstone also created Theatresports – an improv competition format.
history.del_close: Del Close invented the Harold format – a long-form improv piece based on themes rather than sketches. He worked at Second City and ImprovOlympic (now iO). It's said that through his teaching, he literally changed the face of comedy.
history.commedia_dellarte: Commedia dell'arte – a 16th-century Italian form of street theatre – is one of the oldest ancestors of modern improv. Actors played fixed character types (Arlecchino, Pantalone) and improvised dialogue based on a rough scenario outline.
history.io_chicago: ImprovOlympic (now iO Chicago) was founded in 1981 by Charna Halpern and Del Close. This is where the Harold became the official long-form format, and stars like Mike Myers and Amy Poehler began their careers.
history.ucb_founding: Upright Citizens Brigade Theatre (UCB) was founded in 1999 in New York by Amy Poehler, Matt Walsh, Matt Besser, and Ian Roberts – all iO Chicago alumni. UCB popularized a short, 'game of the scene'-based approach to improv.
history.theatresports: Theatresports – a competitive improv format – was invented by Keith Johnstone in the 1970s in Calgary. Today it operates in over 30 countries as a structured improv competition.
history.second_city_toronto: The Second City Toronto, opened in 1973, produced Mike Myers, Dan Aykroyd, Jim Carrey, and Martin Short. Canada became as important a center for improv as Chicago.
history.groundlings: The Groundlings in Los Angeles, founded in 1974 by Gary Austin, produced SNL stars Kristen Wiig, Will Forte, Maya Rudolph, and Darrell Hammond.
history.whose_line: The TV show 'Whose Line Is It Anyway?' (1988 UK, 1998 USA) brought short-form improv to mass audiences. It was a pivotal moment in popularizing improv beyond theatres.
history.harold_origin: The Harold (long-form format) was created by Del Close in the mid-1960s in San Francisco. Its name comes from a joke: when improvisers asked what the format was called, Del would answer 'Harold' – and it stuck.
history.chicago_vs_ny: Chicago-style improv (iO, Second City) emphasizes long form, relationships, and 'playing from reality'. New York style (UCB) is built around the 'game of the scene' concept – finding and escalating a repeating pattern of behavior.
history.annoyance_theatre: The Annoyance Theatre in Chicago, founded in 1987 by Mick Napier, contributed to narrative improv and the 'punk improv' aesthetic – rawer, more unconventional, and bolder in subject matter.

technique.yes_and: "Yes, and..." is the foundational principle of improv: accept what your partner offers ("yes") and build on that reality ("and..."). Blocking – contradicting what your partner said – destroys the scene and the relationship.
technique.offer: Every action and word on stage is an offer – an invitation for your partner to build reality together. A good improviser notices offers and responds to them, rather than imposing their own ideas.
technique.status: Status is how a character perceives themselves in relation to others. High status: calm, slow, controlling space. Low status: chaotic, evasive, fast movements. Status conflicts drive scenes.
technique.endowment: Endowment means giving your partner or an object a quality or history. Instead of saying 'nice sweater', say 'is that the sweater your grandmother was knitting for two years?' – and the scene comes alive.
technique.game_of_scene: The "Game of Scene" is a recurring, unusual pattern of behavior or absurd logic in the scene. When you discover the game, play it consciously – escalate and develop it, rather than escaping to new ideas.
technique.crow: CROW stands for Character, Relationship, Objective, and Where. Establishing all four elements early in a scene gives improvisers a solid foundation from which to build a story.
technique.base_reality: Base Reality – a UCB term – means the normal world of the scene before the 'game' appears. The more natural and convincing the base reality, the better the absurdity works when it arrives.
technique.callbacks: A callback is a return to an earlier element of the scene or show – a word, gesture, or idea – that suddenly gains new meaning in a new context. Callbacks create cohesion and reward audience attention.
technique.patterns: In the Harold format, action is divided into three rounds. In each round, themes and characters from different scenes begin to unexpectedly connect. This 'pattern' technique makes the show feel crafted and brilliantly planned.
technique.first_unusual_thing: UCB principle: the 'first unusual thing' in a scene is the starting point for the game. If your partner says 'My boss is a cat' – that's where the game is. Don't ignore it. Explore it.
technique.emotional_truth: Emotional truth is Viola Spolin's principle: an actor doesn't need to know how to perform an emotion – they need to feel it. That's why Spolin's exercises prioritize 'focus' (a point of concentration) over technique – naturalness comes from engagement, not imitation.
technique.physicality: Viola Spolin believed the body is the primary instrument of the improviser. Working with imaginary objects and space – so-called 'space work' – builds scene concreteness that others can build upon.
technique.avoidance_of_questions: Questions on stage are often a 'laziness trap' – they shift the burden of the offer onto your partner instead of giving something yourself. Rule: instead of asking 'Where are we?', say 'Stunning views from this peak on Kilimanjaro'.
technique.specificity: Specificity saves scenes. Not 'some car' but 'a 1987 mustard-yellow Fiat'. Not 'many years ago' but 'in 1974'. Specificity creates a world, and a world engages.
technique.sweep_edit: The sweep is a scene-cutting technique: one actor enters sweeping their arm like a broom, all others exit. A new scene begins immediately. Good edit pacing is the key to show pacing.
technique.tag_out: A tag-out is a cut where an actor enters and taps another's shoulder, taking their place in the scene. The new person can play the same character in a new context or a completely new character.
technique.support_and_explore: The 'support and explore' principle: before proposing a new direction, make sure you've responded to what your partner just offered. Improv is first about attention, then creativity.
technique.naming_partner: Name your partner early in the scene. It's one of the most powerful tools – it gives them an identity, builds the relationship, and signals to the audience how to see them. 'Hey Mark, you're late again' – and the scene exists.

tips.listen_first: Listen before you speak. Most problems in improv come from playing out your own idea instead of reacting to what's actually happening on stage.
tips.make_partner_look_good: Your only job is to make your partner look great. If everyone thinks that way, the magic appears on its own.
tips.commit_fully: Don't suggest – declare. Enter every idea 100%. A half-hearted absurdity is neither funny nor moving. Full commitment makes the scene.
tips.slow_down: Slow down. When you feel the scene slipping away, slow down and stay with what you have. Rushing is often an escape from genuine emotion.
tips.avoid_denial: Denial destroys scenes. If your partner says 'Do you see that dinosaur?' and you reply 'That's not a dinosaur, it's a cow' – you've just killed the impulse, the trust, and the story simultaneously.
tips.play_to_intelligence: Play to the intelligence of your audience. Avoid obvious jokes and bland solutions. Audiences reward surprises and precision.
tips.dont_plan: Don't plan what you'll say. Planning disconnects you from the present moment. Trust your impulses – what you say without thinking is often the most authentic and surprising.
tips.be_changed: Let the scene change you. If your partner just said something important, let it affect you. Emotional change is more interesting than steadfastness.
tips.trust_the_ensemble: Trust the group. One person shouldn't save the show. Wait for impulses, follow them, be part of the system rather than a solo star.
tips.object_work: Work with objects precisely – remember their size, weight, how you hold them. Consistent imaginary object work shows respect for your partner and your audience.
tips.follow_your_gut: Your first 'yes' is usually right. The second idea – the one that 'seems safer' – is often worse. An improviser's intuition is built through years of work. Trust it.
tips.begin_in_middle: Start a scene mid-action, not with 'Hey, how are you?'. Enter in the middle of conflict, emotion, the moment. Delaying entry into the game wastes precious time.
tips.name_the_relationship: Name the relationship as early as possible. 'Mom, I can't believe this' says more than three minutes of dialogue. The relationship is a map – without it, both you and the audience are lost.
tips.sweat_the_small_stuff: Detail is king. If your partner built something – remember it and refer back to it. Even a small callback to an earlier detail creates the feeling of a coherent world.
tips.drop_the_joke: A better joke comes from truth than from trying to be funny. When you chase the joke, you lose the scene. When you're genuine – humor appears as a bonus.

famous.tina_fey: Tina Fey in "Bossypants" describes four rules of improv: (1) Say yes, (2) Say yes, and..., (3) Don't start statements with a negative, (4) There are no mistakes – only opportunities.
famous.del_longform: Del Close used to say: "Trust your impulses. Improv isn't about being funny – it's about being real." Harold became the foundation of long-form improv worldwide.
famous.tina_fey2: Tina Fey spent years as a writer at Saturday Night Live before stepping in front of the camera. In Bossypants she writes that improv taught her the most important rule of teamwork: your job is to make your partner look good. That philosophy became the foundation of her career.
famous.amy_poehler: Amy Poehler started at ImprovOlympic Chicago and later co-founded UCB Theatre in New York. Her autobiography 'Yes Please' (2014) devotes much space to the lessons improv taught her.
famous.bill_murray: Bill Murray never went to acting school. His training began at Second City Chicago in the 1970s. He says improv taught him one thing: 'Be present. Not the past, not the future – here, now.'
famous.stephen_colbert: Stephen Colbert has long maintained that improv saved his life. After losing his father and brothers in a plane crash, he found community and purpose at Second City Chicago. 'Yes, and...' became his life philosophy, not just a technique.
famous.adam_mckay: Adam McKay – director of 'The Big Short' and 'Vice' – co-wrote Second City revues and performed long-form at iO before becoming SNL's head writer. He says improv taught him listening and teamwork.
famous.mike_myers: Mike Myers learned improv at Second City Toronto, then Second City Chicago. The Austin Powers and Dr. Evil characters emerged from audition improvisations – Myers played them 'as a joke', but audiences fell in love.
famous.charna_halpern: Charna Halpern co-founded iO Chicago with Del Close and for decades served as the guardian of the Harold format. She ensured Del Close's teachings survived by documenting them in 'Truth in Comedy' (1994).
famous.johnstone_quote: Keith Johnstone: "I see my students are afraid of looking stupid. I tell them: your entire education taught you that stupidity is failure. In improv, stupidity is a tool. Use it without shame."
famous.gilda_radner: Gilda Radner, one of the first SNL stars, was a Second City Toronto alumna. Her characters – Emily Litella, Roseanne Roseannadanna – were born from improvisation and observation of real people.
famous.ryan_stiles: Ryan Stiles from 'Whose Line Is It Anyway?' was for years considered one of the fastest improvisers in the world. His rule: 'Never say NO. Even if you don't know what to say – enter and do something, anything.'

yes_and.def: The fundamental improv principle, accept your partner's offer (yes) and add new information to it (and). The engine of collaborative storytelling.

offer.def: Any action, line, or choice that establishes information in a scene. A strong offer gives your partner something clear to respond to.

block.def: Refusing or negating a partner's offer. Blocking stops the scene and forces your partner to start over, draining energy.

crow.def: Character, Relationship, Objective, Where, the four elements that ground a scene. Establishing them quickly gives the audience and performers a shared reality.

status.def: The relative power or social position between characters. Status is fluid and can shift through eye contact, posture, speech, and silence.

justification.def: Accepting an unexpected offer or mistake and making it make sense within the world of the scene. Justification turns accidents into gifts.

endowment.def: Giving another performer a specific quality, history, or emotion through your words or behavior, 'How long have you been a vet?' instantly creates a character.

pimping.def: Deliberately putting a scene partner in an awkward or difficult position on stage. Used sparingly in games; overuse undermines trust.

harold.def: A long-form format invented by Del Close. Three rounds of three scenes each, separated by group games, all branching from a single audience suggestion.

game_of_scene.def: The unusual, repeatable pattern at the heart of a scene. The game is found, named (internally), and then heightened each time it recurs.

heightening.def: Escalating the unusual element of a scene, making it more extreme, more specific, or stranger each time it repeats. The opposite of backing off.

platforming.def: The opening phase of a scene where performers establish information (who, what, where) before the unusual element, the game, has fully emerged.

second_beat.def: In long-form, returning to the same characters or situation from an earlier scene, usually to develop or complicate what was established.

callback.def: Returning to a specific detail, joke, or character established earlier in the show. Callbacks reward attentive audiences and create a sense of wholeness.

reincorporation.def: Bringing back details planted earlier in a scene or show to give it a feeling of completeness. What was setup becomes payoff.

la_ronde.def: A long-form structure where scenes share one character, A plays with B, B plays with C, C plays with D, creating a chain of connected scenes.

monoscene.def: A long-form format where the entire show takes place in a single location with a continuous group of characters, no edits, no scene changes.

tilt.def: A major shift in a scene's established reality or rules, often introduced by an edit or a new character. The tilt raises stakes and forces adaptation.

pattern_game.def: A game built on finding an unexpected association or connection, then repeating and varying that pattern. Common in Harold openings.

tag_out.def: An editing technique where a performer taps another out mid-scene and takes their place, often to explore an alternate reality or character.

swipe_edit.def: A performer walks across the stage with a broad sweeping gesture, ending one scene and starting another. Clean, fast, and readable.

time_dash.def: An editing technique that jumps a scene forward or backward in time while keeping the same characters and location.

side_by_side.def: Running two scenes simultaneously in parallel, cutting between them. The juxtaposition creates meaning that neither scene would have alone.

sweep_edit.def: A large arcing arm gesture that signals the clear end of a scene. One of the most universally recognized stage edits.

walk_on.def: A performer enters an existing scene to add information, energy, or a new character, then exits cleanly once the offer is made.

button.def: The final moment that ends a scene with strong punctuation, a callback, a physical gag, or a line that makes it clear the scene is over.

run.def: A rapid sequence of very short scenes (sometimes just a few seconds each) linked by a theme, location, or character. Used to heighten a pattern at pace.

object_work.def: The physical mime of real or imagined objects in a scene. Specific, consistent object work grounds scenes and raises the perceived reality.

space_object.def: A mimed or invisible physical object agreed upon and used by performers. Space objects become real through consistent handling.

grounding.def: Establishing a clear physical reality at the start of a scene through specific object work, body position, and environmental detail.

scene_painting.def: Verbally describing the environment, often while miming interaction with it, to build a shared physical world for performers and audience.

initiation.def: The first moment of a scene that establishes who, what, or where. A strong initiation gives the scene a clear starting point and direction.

harold.name: Harold
harold.description: A long-form improv format in three acts, starting from a single word suggestion. Scenes and patterns return and connect across the Harold's roughly 40-minute runtime.
harold.rules:
Get one word from the audience
Opening: the group explores the word through free associations, movements, or abstract scenes, no full narratives yet
Round 1: three short two-person scenes, establish new characters, locations, and relationships
Group games (ensemble patterns) are played between rounds
Round 2: revisit Round 1 characters in continued or new situations
Round 3: scenes begin to call back earlier material and converge toward a unified ending

armando.name: Armando
armando.description: A format with a storytelling narrator. The narrator shares a true personal story, then players perform scenes inspired by it. The format alternates between narrator monologues and scenes.
armando.rules:
One player (the Armando) opens with a true personal monologue, no fiction
Players perform scenes inspired by themes, images, or emotions from the story, not a literal retelling
The Armando returns between scenes to continue or begin a new monologue
Alternate monologues and scenes for the full run
Scenes should find the universal truth in the personal story

montage.name: Montage
montage.description: A series of loosely connected scenes inspired by a single theme or word. Each scene is independent, the emphasis is on variety and rapid transitions.
montage.rules:
Get a theme or word from the audience
Perform a series of short, independent scenes, no narrative continuity required
Variety is the goal: mix genres, styles, and scene lengths
Players may call back earlier images or themes in later scenes
Transitions should be fast, keep the energy high throughout

deconstruction.name: Deconstruction
deconstruction.description: An advanced format where an opening scene is replayed and reexamined from different angles, temporal, emotional, narrative. Requires excellent group communication.
deconstruction.rules:
Perform one opening scene inspired by the audience suggestion
Deconstruct and replay the scene from different angles: before/after in time, different emotional register, genre shift, or another character's viewpoint
Each deconstruction should reveal something new hidden in the original material
No two replays should be identical, find what was unseen
The group may converge back or let the material evolve freely

maestro.name: Maestro
maestro.description: One player acts as the maestro, pointing to performers and calling changes in real time, switching emotions, styles, or scenes. A highly dynamic and entertaining format.
maestro.rules:
One player is the Maestro and stands to the side of the stage
The Maestro points to players to start scenes and can end them at will
The Maestro can call mid-scene commands: change emotion, switch genre, trade places, freeze
Players must follow Maestro calls immediately with no hesitation
The Maestro controls pacing and variety, keep the show moving

movie.name: The Movie
movie.description: The group performs an improvised feature film in a given genre, complete with narrative structure, plot twists, and an ending.
movie.rules:
Get a film genre from the audience (e.g. horror, romantic comedy, western)
Establish a clear protagonist with a goal and an obstacle in the first scenes
Play through a full narrative arc: setup → rising action → crisis → climax → resolution
Use genre conventions: music stings, montages, slow motion, dramatic reveals
Aim for a satisfying ending that honours the genre

living_room.name: Living Room
living_room.description: A simple, accessible format: players sit in a living room setting and improvise everyday scenes. Focus on relationships and subtle moments, ideal for beginner groups.
living_room.rules:
No suggestion needed, or use a simple word
Players sit or stand in a 'living room' setting
Play quiet, realistic, everyday scenes, focus on listening and subtlety
Avoid big physical comedy; prioritise emotional truth and relationship dynamics
Ideal for beginner groups or as a warm-up format

revolver.name: Revolver
revolver.description: Each player receives a specific character and rotates through scenes with different partners. The format explores how the same character behaves in different contexts.
revolver.rules:
Get a character type or relationship from the audience
Each player chooses or is assigned a specific character before the show begins
Players rotate through paired scenes with different partners
The same character must remain consistent across all scenes, same want, quirk, and voice
The caller or director signals when to rotate; the format reveals how one character is shaped by different relationships

micetro.name: Micetro
micetro.description: A competitive format where the audience scores scenes and players are gradually eliminated. The last player standing becomes the Micetro, great for shows.
micetro.rules:
All players start on stage; the audience is the judge
Any player(s) can step forward and start a scene; others may join
After each scene, the audience votes, lowest scorer(s) sit down
The host/emcee manages voting and keeps the game moving
The last player standing is crowned the Micetro

hot_spot.name: Hot Spot
hot_spot.description: One player stands center stage and improvises a song. When they run dry, another player tags in. An exercise in musicality and courage, no suggestion needed.
hot_spot.rules:
No suggestion needed
One player steps to center stage and begins singing a song on any topic
When another player is inspired by a word or image in the song, they tap in and start their own song
The tagged player immediately steps back; there should be no gap between songs
Keep energy and flow constant, silence is the enemy

narrative.name: Narrative
narrative.description: Players build a story together with clear narrative structure: hero, goal, obstacle, transformation. Focus on dramaturgy and character development.
narrative.rules:
Get a location from the audience
Establish a clear protagonist with a specific goal in the first scene
Play through the classic narrative arc: setup → obstacle → rising stakes → climax → resolution
Use at least one clear antagonist or conflicting force
Every scene should move the story forward, no filler

time_dash.name: Time Dash
time_dash.description: A scene jumps through time, forward or backward. Players explore how the same relationship looked 10 years ago or will look 10 years from now.
time_dash.rules:
Get a relationship from the audience
Start in the present: play a scene that establishes the relationship
Time-jump forward or backward at director or group cue
Each time period should reveal something new about the relationship
Explore: how did they meet? Where will they be in 20 years? What was the turning point?

perspective.name: Perspective
perspective.description: The same event is replayed multiple times, each time from a different character's perspective, revealing how POV changes meaning.
perspective.rules:
Get an event or situation from the audience
Play the event once from one character's point of view
Replay the same event from a different character's perspective, same facts, different experience
Repeat for each character's angle
A final scene or debrief may show how different perspectives can co-exist

soap_opera.name: Soap Opera
soap_opera.description: A melodramatic format with exaggerated emotions and plot twists. Players improvise an episode of an ongoing series full of dramatic revelations.
soap_opera.rules:
Get a theme from the audience
Play multiple connected characters in an ongoing dramatic serial
Each scene should end on a revelation, cliffhanger, or emotional peak
Embrace melodrama: love triangles, betrayals, secrets, dramatic entrances
Callbacks to earlier scenes are essential, everything must be connected

bat.name: BAT
bat.description: Character, Action, Theme, a short form for 2–4 players. One suggestion sentence generates a scene with a clear character (C), action (A), and theme (T).
bat.rules:
Get a short suggestion sentence from the audience (e.g. 'two friends at a train station')
Identify the core Character (C), Action (A), and Theme (T) from the suggestion
Play the scene: embody the character, pursue the action, and let the theme emerge organically
Keep scenes short (3–7 min) and focused on the core suggestion
Works best with 2 players; 3–4 possible with clear role division

movie_pitch.name: Movie Pitch
movie_pitch.description: Players pitch and perform movie concepts in a given genre. 'Producers' can intervene at any moment. A highly dynamic and humorous format.
movie_pitch.rules:
Get a film genre from the audience
Players take turns pitching movie concepts in that genre (10–30 seconds each)
Other players act as studio executives who can approve, redirect, or interrupt
When a pitch is approved, the group performs a short scene from that movie
Producers may call 'cut' or 'recast' at any time

dream.name: Dream
dream.description: A surrealist format inspired by dream logic. Scenes can be fragmented, symbolic, poetic, normal logic doesn't apply. Requires courage and trust.
dream.rules:
Get an emotion from the audience
Enter dream logic: normal cause-and-effect does not apply
Scenes may dissolve, repeat, or transform without explanation
Players may shift characters, timelines, or settings mid-scene
Follow images and impulses rather than story logic, let the emotion guide the whole show

organic_narrative.name: Organic Narrative
organic_narrative.description: A format where narrative emerges organically from the group, no pre-set structure. Players listen deeply and build the story together by following impulses.
organic_narrative.rules:
Get a theme from the audience
No pre-set structure, the group builds the show in real time
Listen deeply: support the narrative that wants to emerge from the ensemble
Any player may initiate a scene, repeat a scene, or heighten a moment
The show ends when the group feels the story is complete, no director calls it

principles.title: Improv Principles
principles.subtitle: Flash cards for core improv foundations

yes_and.name: Yes, And
yes_and.text: Accept what your partner offers and build on it. Never deny or block what has been established. The scene grows from mutual agreement.
yes_and.example: If your partner says 'Nice dog!', don't say 'I don't have a dog', say 'Yes, she's been acting weird since the accident.'

make_partner_look_good.name: Make Your Partner Look Good
make_partner_look_good.text: Your only job is to make your partner look brilliant. When both players do this, the whole scene rises. Ego kills scenes; generosity builds them.

listen.name: Listen Actively
listen.text: Listen with your whole body, not just your ears. Most mistakes in improv come from not truly receiving what your partner just gave you.
listen.example: Don't plan your next line while your partner speaks, let their words land first.

trust.name: Trust Your Partner
trust.text: Assume your partner's choices are intentional and brilliant. Play with faith, not control. The moment you try to steer, you stop listening.

commit.name: Commit Fully
commit.text: Half-hearted choices kill scenes. Whatever you do, do it 100%. A bad idea fully committed is better than a good idea done timidly.
commit.example: If you're playing a doctor who is afraid of blood, be TERRIFIED, not mildly uncomfortable.

dont_try_funny.name: Don't Try to Be Funny
dont_try_funny.text: Funny comes from truth and commitment, not from jokes. When you chase laughs, you lose the scene. Play honestly and the comedy takes care of itself.

be_present.name: Be Present
be_present.text: Let go of what just happened and stop planning what comes next. The scene exists only in this moment, and your best offers come from full presence.

mistakes_gifts.name: Mistakes Are Gifts
mistakes_gifts.text: If something goes wrong, play it as if it was meant to happen. There are no mistakes in improv, only unexpected offers waiting to be accepted.
mistakes_gifts.example: You forget a character's name mid-scene? Your character just had a memory lapse, play it.

be_obvious.name: Be Obvious
be_obvious.text: Your first instinct is usually the right one. Don't overthink or try to be clever. The most obvious choice is often the most honest and relatable.
be_obvious.example: The scene is set in a hospital, play a doctor or a patient, not a secretly alien janitor.

support_team.name: Support Your Team
support_team.text: Ensemble over ego. Make choices that serve the group's story, not your own spotlight. The best players are often the ones you barely notice.

point_of_view.name: Point of View
point_of_view.text: Every character has a specific attitude toward the world. Commit to one clear perspective and let it color everything your character says and does.
point_of_view.example: A character who believes 'nobody can be trusted' will interpret every kindness as manipulation.

pursue_want.name: Pursue a Want
pursue_want.text: Your character must want something in every scene. Without a want, there's no scene, just pleasant chit-chat. Drive the scene with desire.
pursue_want.example: Even a mundane scene about coffee becomes interesting if one character desperately needs it and the other keeps delaying.

react_specifically.name: React Specifically
react_specifically.text: Vague reactions kill scenes. When something happens, respond with a precise emotion, thought, or physical action. Generic reactions signal you're not really listening.
react_specifically.example: Not 'Wow, that's surprising' but 'I can't believe you used the good scissors on cardboard.'

use_body.name: Use Your Body
use_body.text: Character lives in the body before it lives in the words. Physicality tells the audience who you are before you speak. Don't neglect the instrument.

status_everything.name: Status is Everything
status_everything.text: Every relationship has a status dynamic. Know where you stand relative to your partner at all times and let it inform every choice you make.

play_emotions.name: Play Real Emotions
play_emotions.text: Don't indicate emotions, feel them. Real emotion in the body produces honest, watchable theater. Performed emotion reads as hollow.

relationships_define.name: Relationships Define Characters
relationships_define.text: We are who we are because of who we're in relationship with. Establish your relationship early and let it drive the scene forward.
relationships_define.example: Two strangers have no history. Two estranged siblings have infinite history. Mine that.

status_relative.name: Status is Relative
status_relative.text: You can't have high status without someone having low status. Status only exists in relationship to others, and it shifts constantly throughout a scene.

status_shifts.name: Status Shifts
status_shifts.text: Status is not fixed. Watch for the moments when status changes hands, these are often the most dramatic and satisfying moments in improv.
status_shifts.example: A student corrects the professor. A child refuses to obey. The gardener knows a secret the king does not.

low_status_fun.name: Low Status is Fun
low_status_fun.text: Playing low status is often more interesting than playing high. The underdog, the bumbler, the subservient character, these connect deeply with audiences.

status_in_body.name: Status Lives in the Body
status_in_body.text: High status: still, takes up space, direct eye contact. Low status: fidgety, avoids gaze, collapses inward. The body communicates status before a word is spoken.

edit_at_height.name: Edit at the Height
edit_at_height.text: End a scene when it's at its best, not when it's dying. Leave the audience wanting more. The hardest skill in improv is knowing when you're done.
edit_at_height.example: If the scene just landed its best laugh or most emotional moment, that's your cue to edit.

sweep_momentum.name: Use Momentum to Edit
sweep_momentum.text: A sweep edit carries the energy of the current scene into the next. The ending informs the beginning. Let the emotion travel across the edit.

callbacks_reward.name: Callbacks Reward Attention
callbacks_reward.text: Bringing back an earlier moment rewards attentive audience members and creates satisfying structure. Callbacks say: we were building something all along.
callbacks_reward.example: The muffin from scene one becomes the murder weapon in scene three.

end_scenes.name: Know When to End
end_scenes.text: A scene that overstays its welcome hurts the whole show. Edit decisively. Better to end a moment too soon than a minute too late.

dont_over_edit.name: Don't Over-Edit
dont_over_edit.text: Constant edits interrupt flow and exhaust audiences. Give scenes room to breathe and develop. An unedited, slow-building scene can be the most powerful in the show.

follow_follower.name: Follow the Follower
follow_follower.text: Leadership in an ensemble is shared and fluid. Follow whoever is leading right now, and step up when the group needs you. No one person drives the Harold.
follow_follower.example: If someone starts moving slowly, the whole ensemble slows. If someone starts chanting, others join.

give_take.name: Give and Take
give_take.text: Know when to step forward and when to step back. An ensemble in balance feels effortless. Pushing forward when you should step back creates traffic jams.

group_mind.name: Group Mind
group_mind.text: The ensemble functions as a single creative entity when it's working well. The best ensembles think together without needing words. Trust the shared instinct.

take_care.name: Take Care of Each Other
take_care.text: On stage and off. Look out for your partners. An ensemble built on genuine trust takes bigger risks and recovers from mistakes faster.

agree_loud.name: Agree Out Loud
agree_loud.text: When you accept an offer, say so physically and vocally. Your partner needs to know you've received what they gave. Silence can feel like rejection.
agree_loud.example: Echo a word, mirror a movement, or simply say 'Yes.' Make your acceptance visible.

support_initiations.name: Support Strong Initiations
support_initiations.text: When someone makes a bold offer, get behind it immediately. The ensemble's job is to make the initiator look like a genius, not to compete with them.

use_whole_stage.name: Use the Whole Stage
use_whole_stage.text: Don't cluster in the center. Use depth, corners, and different heights. Stage pictures are as important as dialogue. Empty space is a choice.

share_scene.name: Share the Scene
share_scene.text: Keep focus balanced. Don't upstage your partner or hide in the background. Both performers should be visible and connected at all times.

second_beats.name: Second Beats Go Deeper
second_beats.text: The second scene between the same characters goes deeper than the first. Resist the temptation to reset. Explore the relationship further.
second_beats.example: The siblings argued in round one. In round two, we find out what the argument was really about.

silence_funny.name: Silence is Funny
silence_funny.text: Don't rush to fill silence with words. A long pause after a great line lets laughter breathe and often generates more laughs than the next line would.

simple_agreements.name: Simple Agreements Build Worlds
simple_agreements.text: Two players agreeing on small, specific details builds a richer world than elaborate exposition. 'This kitchen smells like garlic' is better than three paragraphs.
simple_agreements.example: 'It's cold in here.' / 'It's always cold in here.', two lines that build an entire shared history.

strong_offers.name: Make Strong Offers
strong_offers.text: Give your partner something specific to react to. Vague offers force your partner to do all the creative work. Specificity is generosity.
strong_offers.example: Not 'I have something for you' but 'I kept the letter you wrote and never sent.'

label_relationship.name: Label Relationships Early
label_relationship.text: Tell the audience who you are to each other in the first 30 seconds. A relationship label unlocks the whole scene immediately.
label_relationship.example: 'I can't believe you called Mom' is one line that establishes siblings, a family conflict, and an absent third character.

justify.name: Justify Everything
justify.text: Whatever happens on stage, find a reason for it to be true in this world. Don't deny the unexpected, justify it and move forward. Everything can make sense.

heighten_explore.name: Heighten and Explore
heighten_explore.text: Find the unusual thing in the scene and make it more so. Identify what's strange and keep turning up the dial. Explore before you heighten.
heighten_explore.example: The character flinches every time someone says the word 'Tuesday', explore why, then heighten it.

find_game.name: Find the Game
find_game.text: Every scene has a game, the unusual behavior or dynamic that the audience wants to see explored. Finding and naming it (internally) unlocks the whole scene.

genres.title: Genre Style Cards
genres.subtitle: Tips for playing any genre on stage

horror.name: Horror
horror.tip1: Move slowly and deliberately, never rush. Dread is built in pauses, not speed.
horror.tip2: React to sound and shadow before the actual threat. Fear is anticipation.
horror.tip3: Speak in short, clipped sentences. Your character processes the world in fragments.
horror.tip4: Find one specific thing to be terrified of and stay terrified of it consistently.
horror.tip5: Avoid winking at the audience, let the absurdity arise naturally from full commitment.

western.name: Western
western.tip1: Wide stance, slow drawl, deliberate movement. Nobody in a Western is in a hurry (until they are).
western.tip2: Respect is earned, not given. Status is established through action and reputation, not words.
western.tip3: The landscape is always a character, reference it, suffer in it, draw strength from it.
western.tip4: Moral codes are black and white on the surface and complicated underneath.
western.tip5: Silence speaks louder than dialogue. The best Western moments live in the pause before the draw.

film_noir.name: Film Noir
film_noir.tip1: Your character is always being watched and knows it. Paranoia lives beneath every interaction.
film_noir.tip2: Narrate in your head even if you don't say it out loud. Everything has subtext.
film_noir.tip3: Nobody is purely good or bad, moral grey areas are the genre's home territory.
film_noir.tip4: Describe the environment: shadows, lamplight, rain-soaked streets, smoke-filled rooms.
film_noir.tip5: The past always catches up. Every character has a backstory that wants to destroy them.

musical.name: Musical
musical.tip1: Emotion drives the impulse to sing. When feeling becomes too big for speech, that's the song cue.
musical.tip2: Commit to melody and rhythm even if it's imperfect, confidence sells a musical number.
musical.tip3: Every song has a clear want, what is your character trying to express or achieve right now?
musical.tip4: Make eye contact with scene partners and the audience during numbers, it's a shared experience.
musical.tip5: The world is heightened but internally consistent, love, loss, joy, and longing are always real.

documentary.name: Documentary
documentary.tip1: Every character has a thesis, a belief about themselves or the world the doc is capturing.
documentary.tip2: Look directly at the camera (or audience) during interview segments, it breaks the fourth wall intentionally.
documentary.tip3: Contradict yourself. Say one thing and do another. The documentary catches you being yourself.
documentary.tip4: Jargon and expertise signal authenticity, be an expert in something deeply specific.
documentary.tip5: The fly-on-the-wall scenes should feel unscripted, messy, and alive, the opposite of polished.

sci_fi.name: Sci-Fi
sci_fi.tip1: Normal things are extraordinary here, react to technology with matter-of-fact acceptance. It's only strange to the audience.
sci_fi.tip2: Every character has a relationship to power: corporate, governmental, or technological.
sci_fi.tip3: The ethical question always lurks: should we have built this? What does it cost?
sci_fi.tip4: Physicality shifts, gravity might differ, bodies might work differently, time might feel strange.
sci_fi.tip5: Find the human story inside the speculative premise. Sci-fi is always about us, right now.

romance.name: Romance
romance.tip1: Obstacles create desire. The harder it is to be together, the more the audience wants it.
romance.tip2: Subtext is everything, what characters don't say matters as much as what they do.
romance.tip3: Specificity is romantic, not 'I like you' but 'I like the way you do that specific thing.'
romance.tip4: The body leads the feelings. Physical awareness between characters should be palpable.
romance.tip5: Earn the resolution, establish conflict early, let connection build slowly, don't rush the payoff.

action.name: Action
action.tip1: Stakes must be life-or-death (or feel that way). Everything is urgent, everything matters.
action.tip2: Move with purpose, no meandering. Every physical choice should look like a decision.
action.tip3: The wisecracks come after the danger, not during. Timing is everything.
action.tip4: Relationships are forged in crisis, the partner you trust with your life is the one you argue with constantly.
action.tip5: Let the aftermath breathe. After the big moment, the adrenaline drop tells the real story.

tips.opening: Two people, one rich relationship. Lay out the problem but don't solve it, this scene is the raw material the rest of the show will mine.
tips.thematic: Entirely new characters and world. The question to answer: what was the opening really about? Attack that theme from a fresh angle.
tips.return1: The opening pair returns. Sharpen the theme. By the end of this revisit the audience should feel what the show is really exploring.
tips.commentary: Game-heavy, heightened scenes that poke at what the opening characters said or did. Think straight-man / absurd-man. Push further each time.
tips.theRun: A cascade of ever-shorter scenes. Callbacks, tangents, anything that sparked earlier. Keep accelerating until you hit breakneck pace.
tips.finale: The opening characters return one last time. Resolve, reframe, or transform the original problem. Weave the threads into a landing.
